title: Bronze Age Brain Surgery: 4,000-Year-Old Child's Skull Found in Uzbekistan Is Oldest in Central Asia
summary: In a stunning archaeological discovery, researchers have unearthed the 4,000-year-old skull of a Bronze Age child bearing unmistakable scars of cranial surgery. Found at the Djarkutan site in southern Uzbekistan, near the Afghan border, the skull belongs to a child who died around age 5 and represents the oldest documented evidence of surgery in Central Asia—and one of the oldest in all of Asia. The procedure, known as trepanation, involves cutting or scraping a hole into the skull. It was practiced across the ancient world, possibly to treat ailments like epilepsy, migraines, or even mental disorders, though the line between medicine and ritual was often blurred. The child's skull shows clear signs that stone or bone tools were used to perform the operation. The skeleton was discovered in April, buried in a single grave alongside a 3-year-old child. The grave dates to the late third millennium BCE, when Djarkutan was a thriving urban center of the Oxus civilization (also called the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex). This Early Bronze Age culture dominated Central Asia from about 2500 to 1500 BCE, renowned for its advanced agriculture and rich material culture. Its decline is thought to have been triggered by climate change that dried up vital rivers. "Djarkutan continues to surprise us," said Enrico Ascalone, an archaeologist at the University of Salento who led the excavation. "A cranial trepanation on a child, four thousand years ago, in Central Asia: until yesterday it was unthinkable. Today it is in our data." Yet the find is as perplexing as it is groundbreaking. The researchers are now grappling with a host of questions: Which group of specialists in the town could have performed such an intervention? What anatomical knowledge did they possess? And why would they operate on a five-year-old? The team hopes further excavations in the coming months will shed light on these mysteries. For now, the tiny skull serves as a poignant testament to the sophistication of ancient peoples—and a humbling reminder that the impulse to heal, even through risky and invasive means, stretches back millennia.
why_it_matters: This skull challenges assumptions about ancient medical abilities, showing that sophisticated and risky operations were attempted on the most vulnerable patients, and underscores the deep human drive to heal, even with limited knowledge.

background_read: Trepanation is one of the oldest known surgical practices, with evidence dating back to the Neolithic period (around 10,000 BCE) in various parts of the world, including Peru, France, and Africa. In many ancient cultures, opening the skull was believed to release evil spirits or relieve pressure from head injuries. The Oxus civilization, also known as the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC), flourished in what is now Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Afghanistan during the Bronze Age. They built fortified settlements, practiced irrigation agriculture, and traded widely across the Middle East. The Djarkutan site in Uzbekistan is one of the best-preserved BMAC settlements and has yielded many artifacts showing advanced craftsmanship. Around 1500 BCE, the BMAC declined, possibly due to prolonged drought linked to climate change. The discovery of a trepanned child skull there pushes back the timeline of complex surgery in Central Asia and raises questions about the medical knowledge of Bronze Age urban societies. Other examples of trepanation from Asia have been found, but this is the oldest in the region, demonstrating that the practice was more widespread than previously thought.

perspectives.description: The discovery reveals an unexpectedly advanced medical tradition in Central Asia, shifting historical narratives about the development of surgery.
The operation on a five-year-old with stone tools would have been extremely dangerous and painful, raising ethical questions about whether it was more harmful than helpful.
Trepanation was a widespread cross-cultural phenomenon; studying it allows archaeologists to trace shared human responses to illness and injury across continents.
Ongoing excavations at Djarkutan may uncover surgical instruments and more skeletons, potentially clarifying the skill level and social role of ancient healers in the Oxus civilization.
